bounded_statement: Within the supplied files, the report's selected result (two-sample Student t-test, t(46) = -7.67, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = -2.21) was computed by entering all 48 rise readings as separate observations, even though the data description designates jar_id as the independent unit and each of the 12 jars contributes 4 repeated readings from the same batch of dough. The 46 degrees of freedom confirm that 48 rows, not 12 jars, were treated as independent units, so the reported precision (p-value, df, effect size) overstates the evidence available from 12 independent jars. This finding is bounded to the statistical validity of the selected result; the direction of the rye-versus-spelt difference is consistent at the jar level and is not itself contested.

counterevidence_considered.description: The report transparently discloses the clustered design (12 jars, 4 readings each), so the repeated-entry structure is not concealed; however, disclosure does not change the fact that the statistical procedure itself treats the 48 rows as independent.
counterevidence_considered.observed_value: 12 jars, 4 readings per jar disclosed in the report

counterevidence_considered.description: The direction and rough magnitude of the effect are robust: every spelt jar's readings exceed the corresponding rye jars' readings at comparable hours (e.g., all spelt readings at hour 24 are 25-32 mm versus 19-25 mm for rye), so a correct jar-level analysis would likely still find spelt rising higher; this limits the harm to inflated precision (df, p, d) rather than a wrong sign, but does not make the reported t(46) inference valid.

extensions.x-stage1-falsification-attempt: I tried to falsify the finding in three ways. (1) I checked whether the workflow aggregates readings to one value per jar before testing (e.g., per-jar means), which would make the row-independent t-test appropriate; it does not — jars_of() counts jars only for the descriptive table, while the test operates on rise_by_flour's per-reading vectors. (2) I checked whether the reported degrees of freedom could correspond to a jar-level analysis: a jar-level test would give t(10), but the report states t(46), matching 48 rows entered individually, and the report's own Analysis section states outright that all 48 rows were entered as separate observations. (3) I checked whether the data description might designate the reading, not the jar, as the independent unit; it explicitly names jar_id as the independent-unit column and states the four readings per jar come from the same batch of dough. All three checks confirm rather than refute the issue.

root_cause: The workflow pools rise_mm values by flour_type only (rise_by_flour groups on flour_type and discards jar_id for analysis purposes) and passes all per-reading values directly into scipy.stats.ttest_ind, a procedure that assumes each row is an independent observation. No aggregation to jar-level summaries (e.g., per-jar means) and no repeated-measures/mixed model was used, so the four correlated readings per jar were counted as four independent observations each, inflating the effective sample size from 12 jars to 48 rows and hence inflating df (46 instead of 10), deflating the p-value, and distorting Cohen's d.
